topics.title: Adaptive-RAG: a complexity classifier as router
topics.what_it_is: A small classifier (T5-large) predicts one of three levels for the question: A no retrieval, B single-step retrieval, C multi-step retrieval. The label for training comes from which strategy answers right, with dataset bias as a fallback.
topics.why: It is the cleanest published router for RAG. It saves cost on easy questions and keeps accuracy on hard ones.

io.output: label in {A,B,C} and the matching pipeline

steps: Run the three strategies on a training set.
Label each question with the cheapest strategy that was right.
Train the classifier.
At run time classify, then run only that pipeline.
trade_offs: Classifier errors cost accuracy.
Labels are noisy when several strategies are right.

worked_example.spec: Map the real labels: single-hop -> B, bridge and comparison -> C, unanswerable -> check refusal. This mapping is ours (inferred), not from the paper. Count: 8 B, 12 C, 4 unanswerable.

topics.title: Agent memory and tool use
topics.what_it_is: Memory lets the agent keep facts across steps or sessions: short-term (context), long-term (store). MemGPT pages memory in and out like an operating system. HippoRAG 2 uses a graph as long-term memory. Tool use (Toolformer) lets the model call APIs such as search, calculators or SQL.
topics.why: Memory and tools are what make an agent more than a loop of search calls. Router choices are tool choices.
steps: Decide what to write to memory after each step.
Retrieve from memory by similarity or graph.
Choose a tool and call it.
trade_offs: Memory grows and gets stale; tool errors need handling.

topics.title: Agentic RAG: the map
topics.what_it_is: In agentic RAG an LLM agent controls retrieval. It decides whether to search, what to search, whether the result is enough, and when to search again. It can use tools, planning, reflection, memory and other agents.
topics.why: A fixed pipeline retrieves once. An agent can retrieve many times and fix its own mistakes. This helps multi-hop and open questions. It costs more calls and can loop.

io.input: question + tools (vector search, graph search, SQL, web)
io.output: final answer after a loop of think, act, observe

steps: Think: decide what is missing.
Act: call a tool or search.
Observe: read the result.
Repeat or answer; stop at a budget.
trade_offs: Cost and latency grow with the number of steps.
Loops, tool errors and early stopping are common failure modes.

worked_example.spec: Real answer, cost and latency per question exist for a fixed pipeline. Use cost_latency.json as the baseline; an agent run needs a new run (not in the pack).

topics.title: CRAG: corrective retrieval
topics.what_it_is: A light retrieval evaluator scores the retrieved passages as Correct, Incorrect or Ambiguous. Correct: refine the passages (strip irrelevant parts). Incorrect: discard and search the web. Ambiguous: do both.
topics.why: It adds a quality check and a fallback to retrieval without changing the generator.
steps: Score each passage with the evaluator.
Pick the action from the confidence.
Run decompose-then-recompose to keep key sentences.
Generate.
trade_offs: The evaluator needs training; web search brings noise.

worked_example.spec: Context judgments exist per question for the fixed pipeline. Use them as an offline 'correct / incorrect' label example. Check what the judge file holds before use.

topics.title: DRIFT search: dynamic reasoning and inference with flexible traversal
topics.what_it_is: DRIFT starts from community reports (like global search; the primer expands the query with HyDE), generates follow-up questions, and then runs local searches for those follow-ups. It mixes the two modes in one process.
topics.why: It tries to give the breadth of global search with the cost of local search.

io.output: answer from a primer step, follow-up local searches, and a final synthesis

steps: Primer: compare the query with community reports (HyDE-style).
Generate an initial answer and follow-up questions.
Run local search for each follow-up (can recurse).
Synthesise one answer.
trade_offs: No peer-reviewed evaluation exists; the blog reports its own tests.
Iterations are fixed at two in the blog.

topics.title: FLARE: forward-looking active retrieval
topics.what_it_is: The LLM writes the next sentence as a draft. If any token has low probability, the draft is used as a query (low-confidence tokens masked), retrieval runs, and the sentence is rewritten.
topics.why: It retrieves only when the model is unsure, and it uses the plan for the next sentence as the query. Good for long-form output.
steps: Generate a temporary next sentence.
If every token probability >= theta, accept it.
Else retrieve with the sentence (or masked), regenerate.
trade_offs: Needs token probabilities (not every API gives them).
Threshold theta must be tuned.

topics.title: G-Retriever: PCST subgraph plus GNN
topics.what_it_is: G-Retriever retrieves nodes and edges by embedding similarity, then picks a connected subgraph with Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree (PCST). A GNN encodes the subgraph, and a soft prompt plus the textual graph go to the LLM.
topics.why: It keeps the context small and connected. It reduces hallucination on textual graph question answering.
steps: Embed nodes and edges; take top-k by cosine with the query.
Assign prizes; solve PCST with an edge cost.
Encode the subgraph (GAT) into a soft token; add its text.
Generate.
trade_offs: Needs training of GNN and projector; PCST on large graphs costs time.

topics.title: GraphRAG local and global search
topics.what_it_is: Microsoft GraphRAG builds an entity graph, finds communities (Leiden), and writes a summary report per community. Local search starts from entities near the query and adds their edges, text units and community reports. Global search runs map-reduce over community reports to answer questions about the whole corpus.
topics.why: Local search handles specific multi-hop questions. Global search handles 'what are the main themes' questions that vector RAG cannot answer.

io.output: local: context window of entities, relations, text, reports; global: partial answers then one final answer

steps: Link the query to entities.
Local: gather neighbours, text units, community reports by budget.
Global: shuffle reports into chunks, MAP partial answers with a helpfulness score, REDUCE the best into one answer.
trade_offs: Indexing cost is high (many LLM calls).
Global search is slow and costly per query.

worked_example.spec: Real local context windows (3000 estimated tokens: 20% community, 50% text, 30% graph) and a real MAP-REDUCE run exist. Show the budget split and one real global answer. Graph: 662 nodes.

topics.title: HippoRAG: personalized PageRank memory
topics.what_it_is: HippoRAG builds a graph from open information extraction. At query time it links query entities to nodes and runs Personalized PageRank from them. The scores of passages come from the node scores.
topics.why: One graph step can join facts from separate passages. It is cheap compared with iterative LLM retrieval.

symbols.n: personalized distribution: equal mass on the linked query nodes, zero elsewhere
symbols.d: restart probability (damping factor in the paper; 0.5, tuned on 100 MuSiQue examples)
symbols.P: transition matrix of the KG (triple edges plus synonymy edges)

steps: Offline: extract triples with an LLM; build graph and passage-to-node links.
Online: extract query entities; link to nodes.
Run PPR with the linked nodes as the seed distribution.
Rank passages; give the top to the reader.
trade_offs: Entity extraction errors break the graph.
Indexing cost.

worked_example.spec: Real PPR runs per question with damping and top nodes exist. Compare ppr_graph with dense_cosine in runs/metrics_by_method.json per question type.

topics.title: HybridRAG: graph plus vector retrieval
topics.what_it_is: The system runs a vector search and a graph search (entities, relations) for the same question. It concatenates both contexts for the LLM. HybridRAG did this for financial earnings-call text.
topics.why: Vector search finds similar wording. The graph finds structure and multi-hop links. Together they cover each other's gaps.
steps: Embed the query, search the vector index.
Link entities, expand the graph.
Merge or concatenate; rerank or deduplicate.
Generate.
trade_offs: Two indexes to build and keep in sync.
Merge rule is a design choice (concatenate, RRF, weighted).

topics.title: HyDE: hypothetical document embeddings
topics.what_it_is: The LLM writes a fake answer passage. The system embeds that passage, not the question. The fake passage can contain false details, but the encoder acts as a filter: the real passages near it in vector space are retrieved.
topics.why: Question embeddings and answer embeddings live in different regions. An answer-shaped text is closer to the real answer passage. HyDE needs no relevance labels.

io.output: embedding v = mean of f(d_k) over N sampled fake documents d_k (optionally plus f(q))

symbols.f(q): query itself, added to the average (Eq. 8)

steps: Sample N fake documents with an instruction-following LLM.
Embed each with an unsupervised contrastive encoder f and average.
Search the corpus with the average vector.
trade_offs: One generation per query, so latency and cost grow.
Wrong or generic fake text pulls the vector to the wrong area; the benefit is weak when the LLM lacks domain knowledge.

worked_example.spec: 6 real HyDE items (q02,q06,q09,q13,q14,q18). Show the real generated paragraph for q02 (it adds the year 1996 and the author, which the question did not contain) and cosine of gold p005: 0.7202 plain vs 0.8852 with the fake text. Rank changes: 4 unchanged, 1 worse (q14).

topics.title: Iterative retrieval-generation (Iter-RetGen, IRCoT)
topics.what_it_is: The system alternates: generate a draft, use the draft as the next query, retrieve, generate again. Each round improves the query.
topics.why: The first answer shows what is missing. It is a simple form of agentic RAG without a tool router.
steps: Retrieve with the question.
Generate an answer or a reasoning step.
Append it to the query; retrieve again.
Repeat T times.
trade_offs: T times the cost; errors can reinforce.

topics.title: KG-RAG and Think-on-Graph: the LLM walks the graph
topics.what_it_is: The LLM and the knowledge graph work together. In Think-on-Graph the LLM runs a beam search over the graph: at each hop it picks relations and entities, and it stops when the path answers the question.
topics.why: Paths give explainable evidence. They help multi-hop questions where text search fails.
steps: Extract topic entities.
Beam search: prune relations, explore entities, prune again.
Reason with the paths; if enough, answer, else go deeper.
trade_offs: Many LLM calls per hop; needs a good entity link.

worked_example.spec: Real k-hop data: per question, cumulative nodes and passages for k=0..3 with gold found. Show where gold appears first.

topics.title: LightRAG: dual-level retrieval
topics.what_it_is: LightRAG builds a graph with entity and relation descriptions as vector-indexed keys. A query gives low-level keywords (entities) and high-level keywords (themes). Low-level search matches entities and high-level search matches relations. The context joins both and the neighbours.
topics.why: It uses graph and vector together and supports cheap incremental updates (no community re-summary).

io.output: context from entity hits, relation hits and one-hop neighbours

steps: LLM extracts local and global keywords.
Vector search over entity keys and relation keys.
Add one-hop neighbours.
Generate.
trade_offs: Keyword extraction by LLM adds a call; quality of descriptions matters.

topics.title: LLM self-routing: RAG or long context (Self-Route)
topics.what_it_is: The LLM first answers from retrieved chunks and may say 'unanswerable'. Only then the system sends the full document to a long-context model.
topics.why: RAG is cheap, long context is more accurate. The router uses the model's own refusal as the signal.

io.output: RAG answer, or fallback to full-context answer

steps: Run RAG with a prompt that allows 'unanswerable'.
If answerable, keep the answer.
Else call the long-context model.
trade_offs: Depends on honest refusals; costs two calls on hard cases.

worked_example.spec: The pack has 4 unanswerable questions and the top-1 hit of each method on them (unanswerable_top1). Use those to show what a retriever returns when no answer exists.

topics.title: Model routing (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT)

Train a router (similarity-weighted, matrix factorisation, BERT, or LLM).
Set a threshold for the cost-quality point.

topics.title: Multi-query retrieval and RAG-Fusion
topics.what_it_is: The LLM writes several variants of the question. The system retrieves for each variant. It then merges the ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF).
topics.why: One phrasing may miss a passage that another phrasing finds. RRF merges lists without score calibration.

io.output: fused ranking over the union of lists

symbols.rank_i(d): position of d in list i (absent = no term)

steps: Generate n variants (the real example uses 3).
Retrieve top-k for each.
Compute RRF score per passage and sort.
trade_offs: Variants can be near-duplicates; gain is small.
More lists means more retrieval load; k constant of 60 is a convention.

worked_example.spec: 6 real items. First-gold rank after RRF vs original: 4 same, 1 better (q09: 3 to 2), 1 worse (q06: 1 to 2). Show q02 variants: 'LASSO acronym meaning statistics' etc., fused top1 p005 score 0.065574 (= sum of 1/(60+rank), recompute).

topics.title: Query decomposition and multi-hop (least-to-most, self-ask, IRCoT)
topics.what_it_is: A hard question is split into sub-questions. The system answers or retrieves for each, then combines. Least-to-most splits a problem into easier steps. Self-ask lets the model ask itself follow-up questions and call search. IRCoT interleaves retrieval with each chain-of-thought sentence.
topics.why: A bridge question needs two passages. One search for the whole question often finds only one. The graph route handles the same case with an edge between the two entities.

io.output: sub-questions, one retrieval each, fused context or composed answer

steps: Ask the LLM for sub-questions (or let it ask them one by one).
Retrieve for each sub-question.
Fuse lists or feed each answer into the next question.
Compose the final answer.
trade_offs: Errors in sub-question 1 pass to sub-question 2.
More LLM and retrieval calls; no gain for single-hop questions.

worked_example.spec: 4 real decomposition items (q09,q11,q13,q14; all bridge, 2 gold passages). After RRF over the sub-question lists: gold in top-5 both passages for q09 and q11; only one for q13 and q14. Compare with the graph k-hop result on the same questions (graph/khop.json).

topics.demo_hint: Show the question tree, the sub-question retrievals and which gold passage each found.

topics.title: LLM query expansion (query2doc and prompting)
topics.what_it_is: The LLM writes extra text that relates to the query. The system appends this text to the query, then runs sparse (BM25) or dense search. Query2doc writes a pseudo-document from few-shot prompts. Jagerman et al. study several prompts, including chain-of-thought.
topics.why: Sparse search misses words that are not in the query. The LLM adds synonyms and related facts from its own memory. Gains are large for BM25 and smaller for strong dense retrievers.

io.output: expanded query q+ = q repeated n times + generated text d'

steps: Prompt the LLM for a short passage that answers q.
Concatenate q (repeated, so it keeps weight) and d'.
Search with BM25 or an embedding of q+.
trade_offs: The LLM can invent facts and add them to the key (knowledge leakage into retrieval).
Weak gains on well-trained dense retrievers.

worked_example.spec: Use hyde items: compare dense rank of the gold passage with the plain query and with the generated text. Real result: first-gold rank unchanged in 5 of 6, worse in 1 (q14: 1 to 2), better in 0. Recompute from retrieval_original vs retrieval_with_generated.

topics.title: Query rewriting (Rewrite-Retrieve-Read)
topics.what_it_is: A rewriter model turns the user question into a better search query. In Rewrite-Retrieve-Read a small model (T5) is first trained with supervised warm-up, then tuned with reinforcement learning. The reward is the answer quality of the frozen reader LLM.
topics.why: The reader LLM and the retriever are fixed. Only the query is changed. This is the cheapest place to improve a RAG system that you cannot retrain. It also shows the idea of summarising or cleaning the query with a smaller model.

io.output: rewritten query x~ used for retrieval; reader LLM answers from x~ context

steps: Warm up the small rewriter with pseudo-labels (queries that gave a correct answer).
Run the rewriter, search, let the frozen reader answer.
Reward = answer metric (EM/F1) minus a penalty; update the rewriter with PPO.
trade_offs: Needs training data and a reward signal.
The rewriter can drop details the user needed.

worked_example.spec: Use the multiquery items as a proxy: the 3 LLM variants per question are rewrites. Show q02 'What does the name lasso stand for?' with its 3 real variants and the 3 ranked lists.

topics.why: A cheap model for a narrow task cuts cost and latency. The main LLM keeps the budget for the answer.

topics.title: Query understanding and transformation: the map
topics.what_it_is: A user query is often a poor search key. Query understanding changes the query before retrieval. The change can be a rewrite, an expansion, a hypothetical answer, a more general question, several sub-questions, or a structured query such as SQL.
topics.why: The embedding of a short or vague question can sit far from the embedding of the passage that answers it. A transformed query closes that gap. Each transform costs one LLM call and can drift from the user intent.

io.output: one or more search keys: text, hypothetical document, sub-questions, SQL/Cypher, filters

steps: Classify what the question needs (one fact, many facts, an aggregate, a graph path).
Choose a transform: rewrite, expand, HyDE, step-back, decompose, text-to-query.
Retrieve with the new key or keys.
Fuse the result lists (RRF) when there are several keys.
trade_offs: Every transform adds latency and one LLM cost.
A bad transform can lose the user intent (see step-back failure in the real example).

worked_example.spec: 20 real items: hyde 6, multiquery 6, stepback 4, decomposition 4 (embedder all-MiniLM-L6-v2, LLM qwen3.7-plus, temperature 0). Compare first-gold rank before and after per technique. Demo scale, not an evaluation.

topics.title: ReAct: reasoning and acting
topics.what_it_is: The LLM writes a thought, then an action (for example Search[query]), then reads the observation. It repeats until it can answer.
topics.why: ReAct is the base loop of almost every agentic RAG system.

io.output: trajectory of (thought, action, observation) and an answer

steps: Prompt with few examples of the format.
Run the model until it writes an action.
Execute the action, append the observation.
Stop at Finish[answer] or at a step limit.
trade_offs: Errors in a thought mislead later steps.
Prompts can be long.

topics.title: Router between vector RAG and GraphRAG
topics.what_it_is: A router sends each query to vector RAG, GraphRAG, or both. Possible signals: query type (specific vs global), hop count, entity count, or a trained classifier. Published studies show that each method wins on different question types, and they suggest selection or integration.
topics.why: Graph indexing costs more and does not always win. A router uses the graph only where it helps.
steps: Label queries by which method answered right (or by type).
Train or define the rule.
Run only the chosen path; fall back to both if confidence is low.
trade_offs: No standard published router for this exact choice was found; the idea is built from the cited studies and Adaptive-RAG.

worked_example.spec: Per question type, compare dense_cosine, bm25, rrf and ppr_graph (real metrics). The type with a clear winner defines the rule. Compute; do not claim a win from 24 questions.

topics.title: Routing: choosing the retrieval path
topics.what_it_is: A router decides where a query goes: no retrieval, one vector search, iterative multi-step retrieval, a graph search, an SQL database, or the web. The router can be rules, an embedding match, a trained classifier, or an LLM.
topics.why: One path does not fit all questions. Simple questions waste cost on multi-step methods. Complex questions fail on single-step methods.

io.input: query (and cheap features: length, entities, history)

steps: Define the routes and what each one is good at.
Pick the router type (rule, semantic, classifier, LLM).
Measure route accuracy and the cost saved.
Add a fallback route for low confidence.
trade_offs: Router errors send a question to the wrong tool and the system cannot recover.
Labels for training are expensive; weak labels come from which route succeeded.

worked_example.spec: 24 real questions with type labels: 8 single-hop, 8 bridge, 4 comparison, 4 unanswerable. The type is a natural route label. Show which retrieval method scored best per type from runs/metrics_by_method.json (by_question_type).

topics.title: Self-query: extract metadata filters from the question
topics.what_it_is: The LLM splits the question into a semantic part and a structured filter (for example year > 2023, author = X). The vector store applies the filter first, then runs similarity on the semantic part.
topics.why: Similarity search cannot enforce 'only 2024 papers'. A filter can. The metadata comes from parsing.
steps: Describe metadata fields to the LLM.
Generate a structured filter (JSON or a small DSL).
Validate it against the schema.
Search with filter + vector.
trade_offs: Wrong filter silently removes the right passage; always log the filter.

worked_example.spec: Corpus passages carry article, section, oldid and retrieved date. Example: question 'In the ridge regression article, who introduced it?' becomes filter article='Ridge regression'. Show how many of 138 passages remain (recompute).

topics.title: Self-RAG: learned reflection tokens
topics.what_it_is: The LM is trained to output special reflection tokens: Retrieve (should I search?), IsRel (is the passage relevant?), IsSup (does the passage support my sentence?), IsUse (is the answer useful?). At inference these tokens guide beam search over segments.
topics.why: The model decides about retrieval itself and critiques itself. No separate router or grader is needed at run time.

io.output: answer with citations, plus critique tokens

steps: A critic model labels training data with reflection tokens.
Fine-tune the generator on the labelled data.
At run time predict Retrieve; if yes fetch k passages.
Generate per passage, score with critique tokens, choose best segment.
trade_offs: Needs fine-tuning (7B, 13B in the paper).
Critic labels come from GPT-4 in the paper.

worked_example.spec: No training here. Draw one real passage p005 and the four token decisions as an annotated example (constructed).

topics.title: Semantic router and rule/classifier routers
topics.what_it_is: A semantic router stores example utterances for each route. It embeds the query and picks the route whose examples are nearest by cosine similarity. A rule router uses keywords or regex. A classifier router uses a trained model.
topics.why: It is fast (no LLM call) and cheap. It is a common first router in production.
steps: Write 5-20 example utterances per route.
Embed them once.
Embed the query; compare with each route (max or mean cosine).
If best score < threshold, use the default route.
trade_offs: Needs good examples; thresholds drift with the embedding model.

worked_example.spec: Use the 24 real questions as utterances: build centroids per question type with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (raw/embeddings.npz holds question embeddings) and measure leave-one-out route accuracy. Compute; do not guess.

provenance.notes: The 'semantic router' is a library pattern (Aurelio Labs semantic-router), not a paper known to me. The embedding-similarity idea rests on the sentence-embedding papers. No origin paper found; do not invent one.

topics.title: Step-back prompting
topics.what_it_is: The LLM first writes a more general question (a step-back question) about the principle behind the user question. The system retrieves for both the original and the general question and gives both result sets to the reader.
topics.why: Specific questions can hide the concept that the answer needs. A general question finds background passages.

io.output: general question; two retrieval lists (merge or concatenate)

steps: Prompt the LLM with a few examples of step-back questions.
Retrieve for the step-back question and for the original.
Answer with both contexts.
trade_offs: The general question can retrieve only general text and push the exact fact out of the top-k.
Few-shot examples are domain-specific.

worked_example.spec: 4 real items. Step-back query alone: the gold passage left the top-5 in 2 of 4 (q06, q19); improved first-gold rank in 1 (q09: 3 to 1); worse in 1 (q15: 1 to 2). The real q06 step-back text: 'What are the fundamental principles governing the convergence and stability of iterative optimization algorithms?' Fusing with the original (RRF) keeps gold at rank 2 for q06.

Structurizer builds it from the documents.

topics.title: Text-to-Cypher (and graph query generation)
topics.what_it_is: A model turns a question into a Cypher query for a property graph (Neo4j). The graph database runs it. The result is a set of nodes, edges or aggregates.
topics.why: Counting, path and pattern questions over a graph are exact with Cypher. This is the structured alternative to GraphRAG local search.

steps: Give the LLM the schema and few-shot pairs.
Generate Cypher.
Run it; on a syntax or empty result, repair and retry.
Give the rows to the answer step.
trade_offs: Small training sets: Text2Cypher is a young field.
Wrong relation direction or label names are common.

topics.title: Text-to-SQL
topics.what_it_is: A model turns a natural-language question into an SQL query. The database runs the query. The rows go back to the LLM as context. This is retrieval by structure, not by similarity.
topics.why: Aggregates, filters, joins and exact numbers are weak points of vector search. SQL gives exact results. The user's own data problem (tables, not text) is often solved here.
steps: Give the LLM the schema and a few examples.
Generate SQL (decompose hard questions; DIN-SQL does schema linking, classification, generation, self-correction).
Execute, catch errors, retry.
Pass rows (not raw SQL) to the answer step.
trade_offs: Wrong joins or hallucinated columns; execution accuracy drops on large schemas.
Security: run with a read-only role.

worked_example.spec: The real-example pack has no table. A later step can build a small SQLite from graph/stats.json node types (662 nodes, typed edges) and ask 'how many Method nodes' with the real count 224. Recompute with SQL.

topics.title: When vector RAG, GraphRAG or hybrid wins
topics.what_it_is: Vector RAG wins on single-fact, wording-close questions and on cost. GraphRAG wins on multi-hop, relational and corpus-wide summary questions. Hybrid is stronger when both kinds of question appear. Studies also show cases where plain RAG beats GraphRAG.
topics.why: It is the decision rule behind the whole thesis topic. It must be backed by numbers.
steps: List the question types of the use case.
Run both methods on a sample.
Compare accuracy, cost, latency per type.
Choose; route if the mix is mixed.
trade_offs: Results depend on corpus, graph quality and judge model.
Demo-scale numbers here are not an evaluation of the thesis system.

worked_example.spec: Real metrics per type for 12 retrieval methods and answer judgments. Present as demo scale only (24 questions).
